P2-E44-DISCUSSION-CLAUSE: The failure of type 9 is where the derivation says it should be. R1's gap is computed for a leader that brakes at no more than b<sub>max</sub>, and a vehicle that stops dead, a fault rather than a manoeuvre, lies outside that model [14], so a same-direction follower already inside a one-lane segment can come inside the 5 m static margin and, in 7 of 10,000 encounters, touch. A dead-stop margin, the follower's own stopping distance at its current speed, would close the case at a cost in segment capacity; we did not run it, and the count stands as a limit of braking-based separation. The twelve types could not have found the other case the derivation names, a conforming leader that brakes on an uphill grade and so exceeds b<sub>max</sub>, because every one of their encounters is on the flat or downhill. A separate simulation of uphill following found it (Appendix A.4): under R1 as it was, no contact, but followers inside the static margin from 14° on the Moon and 6.5° at Mars gravity when the follower's actuation lags by a second. A slope term in R1 removed every such case when following and left a remainder of at most 0.14 m in the Mars one-lane convoy, which comes from the lag model. We therefore state R1 with the slope term as the proposed rule (Table 2); the twelve types were run without it, on ground where it is inactive. The ring deadlocks of type 5 (0.7 % of the judged encounters under R3 as written, 19.0 % under the keep-one-slot-free variant) are the property noted before the main run [43]: the exit-bay rule is not deadlock-free on a ring of one-lane segments with finite bays, the variant that was meant to help makes it worse, and the logistics model's zero count comes from its unbounded bays; the pooled count stood when the stall classifier was corrected (change 9 of [43]). The landing closure is the second type with a hard violation, found only when it was run on fresh seeds: in 1 of 10,000 encounters a vehicle held at the zone boundary kept its grant for a one-lane resource beyond the zone, and a vehicle inside the zone waited for that resource until after the closure. R5 and R3 are each obeyed and together hold a vehicle where it must not be. The request rule of change 9 of [43] was then run on all 10,000 fresh encounters: it allowed no violation and failed no encounter that had finished, but it was chosen after seeing the violation, so the result is exploratory, and 62 % of these encounters end incomplete under either rule. The main run, on the seeds used to fix the simulator, had not shown the case, which is what the fresh seeds were for. The four deadlocks of type 6 are a gap in the rules: a crossing that lies on a landing zone's boundary can be held by a vehicle stopped at the zone line, and the vehicle leaving the closing zone through it is blocked. R3 keeps a vehicle out of a segment it cannot leave into a bay, but no rule keeps it out of a junction whose far side is a hold point. The repair is a one-line extension of R3's exit check to junctions; we did not run it, and the count stands as found.
P2-E44-COMPARISON-CLAUSE: Our per-type bounds are the zero-numerator bounds of Hanley and Lippman-Hand [33]: with no violation in n encounters the 95 % upper limit is close to 3/n, 3.0 × 10<sup>−5</sup> at 100,000 and 3.0 × 10<sup>−4</sup> at 10,000, larger at the smaller effective n of the weighted types, and they hold for the generated distribution of each type, not for the base's actual traffic. Zhao and colleagues reach rarer events by importance sampling on the lane-change parameters [35]; we used the same device on three types (the exit distance, the crew's emergence time and the dead-stop time), which cost effective sample size (Section 5.6) and found the one violating case, type 9, where the boosted region was.

P2-E45-RESULTS-PARAGRAPH: The four layouts have 47,085 reachable states and 272,899 transitions in all; the largest, a pad visit with two oncoming vehicles and radio links, has 36,912 states. In every layout the search found no state that breaks a safety invariant, no deadlock state, no state from which the goal is unreachable and no livelock component; the longest shortest path to the goal is 41 steps of 8.5 s on 10 m cells. Each mutation produced its counterexample. Without R3's exit-slot check, 2 reachable states of the three-vehicle line are deadlocks and 39 cannot reach the goal (13 livelock components); the shortest deadlock trace is 12 steps. Without R5's entry check, 384 reachable states have a vehicle inside the landing zone while it is closed, the shortest reached in 14 steps. Without R7's hold, 198 reachable states break an invariant (138 in the segment without the reservation, 96 opposite directions in the segment; a state may break both), the shortest in 5 steps. The traces are stored beside the results. H7's second clause as registered asks for a counterexample for each rule removed [43]. It holds for the three rule clauses that were removed, R3's exit slot, R5's entry check and R7's hold; R6 and R10 are also in the discrete model and were not mutated, so the clause is met in part. Development of the checker found four counterexamples before the final run, three in the checker itself (R6 checked as a state invariant rather than on the vehicle's motion, which flagged crew walking up to a stopped vehicle; no crew distance computed on the landing spur, 80 violating states in the first layout; bay slots counted per lane, which hid the R3 mutation) and one in the reading of a rule: with the bays fixed, the three-vehicle line deadlocked when a vehicle granted the segment with a free exit slot lost that slot to a vehicle that drove into the bay afterwards. R3's “reserved for it” therefore binds every other vehicle: a bay counts the slots reserved by segment holders as taken, in the checker and in the encounter simulator alike.

It says nothing about larger layouts, which is where the simulator takes over.

P2-H7-ABSTRACT-CLAUSE: The safety program allowed no violation in eleven of twelve encounter types; the exception, a vehicle stopping dead in a one-lane segment, defeats a gap rule derived for a braking leader; the ring of one-lane segments with finite bays deadlocked in 3.9 % of its encounters, and the landing closure four times in 10,000 at a crossing on the zone boundary. The exhaustive search of 47,085 reachable states found no unsafe or stuck state and caught three removed rules.
P2-CONCLUSION-SAFETY-CLAUSE: The exhaustive check found no unsafe or stuck state in 47,085 reachable states; the simulator found no violation in eleven of twelve encounter types, one in the twelfth, a vehicle that stops dead inside a one-lane segment; the ring of one-lane segments with finite bays deadlocked in 3.9 % of its encounters, and the landing closure four times in 10,000 at a crossing on the zone boundary.
P2-E47-DESIGN-SENTENCE: E44's twelve types at g = 3.71 m/s<sup>2</sup> with the lunar vehicles unchanged, 2,000 encounters per type and 12,000 for types 1 and 7, generated from E44's seeds so that each Mars encounter is paired with the lunar encounter of the same type, batch and index; and E43's ATC and uncoordinated cells at today's fleet, seeds 1–30 (the 2028 label marks the paired lunar runs; the Mars link uses no start year), with a Mars Earth link: round trips of 6, 20 and 44 minutes added to the two hours of staff time per referred conflict, Earth in view for the first 50 % of each sol (Assumed) or, as a variant, continuously through one areostationary relay, a 14-day conjunction from day 200 and two five-day dust storms, both as loss of the Earth link only. 44,000 encounters and 210 runs in seven cells.

P2-E47-INTRO-CLAUSE: On Mars, with the lunar vehicles on the same roads, the safety program behaved as on the Moon, the dead-stop exception included, but only on the flat: at Mars gravity the lunar brakes hold no downhill steeper than 7.7°, so no sloped encounter could be driven. Coordination that depends on Earth lost about one-sixth of what it loses on the Moon, the opposite of what we pre-registered for Mars (H9, Section 4.1): with Earth in view for half of every sol, as we assumed, a referred conflict waits hours, not the days of the polar base's window gaps (Section 5.8).
P2-E47-RESULTS-PARAGRAPH: The Mars part ran E44's twelve types at g = 3.71 m/s<sup>2</sup> with the lunar vehicles, 44,000 encounters paired with the lunar encounters of the same seeds, and E43's two road modes at today's fleet with a Mars Earth link (Tables 7 and 8). The safety program allowed no violation in eleven of the twelve types; in the dead-stop type the following vehicle came inside the 5 m static margin in 11 of 2,000 encounters, the same eleven encounters that violated on the Moon, and no vehicle touched another. With no violation the bound at 2,000 encounters is 2.7 × 10<sup>−3</sup> with the Bonferroni correction (1.5 × 10<sup>−3</sup> without), larger at the effective n of the weighted types; type 9's Clopper–Pearson limit is 1.2 × 10<sup>−2</sup> with the correction (9.1 × 10<sup>−3</sup> without), against 8.1 × 10<sup>−3</sup> (7.2 × 10<sup>−3</sup>) on the Moon at five times the sample. The ring deadlocked under R3 as written in 2 of the 368 encounters in which deadlock is judged (0.5 %; 0.20 % of all 979 driven) and under the variant in 68 of 395 (17.2 %; 6.7 % of 1,021), against 0.7 % and 19.0 % of the judged encounters on the Moon (70 of 2,000 pooled), and the landing closure twice in 2,000 (four in 10,000 on the Moon); no other type deadlocked. Of the 12,000 following draws, 8,961 (74.7 %) were on downhills steeper than 7.7°, the steepest the vehicles' 0.5 m/s<sup>2</sup> service brake holds at Mars gravity (Section 3.5), and were not driven; on the Moon the limit is 16.7–18.0° depending on the friction value, only the 20° draws are excluded, and 3,019 (25.2 %) of the same draws were not driven. No sloped encounter of any type was driven on Mars, and on the flat the braking term of R1 and R2 differs between the bodies by at most 0.014 m/s<sup>2</sup> (at the lowest friction value, where friction and not the service brake binds on the Moon), so the driven Mars encounters repeat the lunar ones with the same seeds. For the 4,411 paired encounters that nominal planners drove to the end on both bodies, the rules delayed the vehicles by 67.0 s on Mars and 66.9 s on the Moon, a ratio of 1.00. The logistics model's ATC mode uses neither gravity nor the Earth link, and its 30 Mars runs equalled E43's ATC runs on every seed. The uncoordinated mode cost 10.4 h [7.8, 13.1 h], 11.1 h [8.5, 14.0 h] and 10.8 h [8.8, 12.8 h] of delay per delivery above the ATC mode at round trips of 6, 20 and 44 minutes without a relay, and 8.2 h, 8.7 h and 6.4 h with the relay (Table 8); at 20 minutes without a relay that is 0.72 of the ATC mode's 15.5 h. On the Moon the same difference was 63.5 h [58.4, 68.9 h] in 2028, 4.1 times the ATC mode's delay, and 82.9 h [76.0, 89.7 h] in 2038 (Table 5); the Mars cost is 0.18 of the Moon's 2028 cost. The Mars fleet referred 94 conflicts a year to Earth and waited 772 h for the decisions, 8.2 h per conflict; the lunar fleet referred 53 and waited 1,969 h, 37.2 h per conflict. H9's first clause, zero violations under Mars gravity, is supported on the flat in the same eleven types as in H7's main run (the Mars encounters were not rerun on fresh seeds), fails in type 9 for the same encounters, and is untested on slopes; its second, a similar rule cost, is tested only by the encounter delays, where it holds; its third, that Earth-dependent coordination loses more on Mars, is contradicted: it loses less in every Mars cell, with intervals that do not overlap the Moon's.
P2-E47-DISCUSSION-CLAUSE: the safety program behaved as on the Moon, the dead-stop exception included, but that is weaker evidence than it looks: the only ground the lunar brakes hold at Mars gravity is nearly flat, and on the flat the braking term is the same on both bodies, so the Mars encounters that were driven repeat the lunar ones; the rules are untested on the slopes where Mars gravity acts. The same holds for the rules' cost, measured only by the paired encounter delays. The Earth-dependent mode lost about one-sixth of what it loses on the Moon, 11.1 h against 63.5 h, the opposite of H9's third clause. The reason is in the Earth windows, not the round trip: the three round trips gave the same cost within their intervals, and the relay lowered the mean at each, while a Mars base, as we modelled it, sees Earth for half of every sol (Assumed, Section 7) and the polar base's computed windows [42] leave it blind for days, so a referred conflict waited 8.2 h for a decision on Mars and 37.2 h on the Moon. The reversal therefore holds for any Mars site whose horizon returns Earth every sol, and would not for one that does not. The Mars fleet referred more conflicts (94 against 53) for the same demand and almost the same deliveries (2,932 against 2,928 items); we have not traced the cause. The one Mars-specific finding is about hardware. The guaranteed braking of Section 3.5 is the smaller of the service brake and the friction limit, less the downhill component: on the Moon the friction term binds at μ = 0.3 and the 0.5 m/s<sup>2</sup> service brake above it, so the holdable downhill is 16.7–18.0°; on Mars the service brake binds at every friction value, so braking does not grow with gravity while the slope term does, and the holdable downhill falls to 7.7°. Of the following draws, 75 % were on steeper ground, against 25 % on the Moon. R2 gives a zero admissible speed on such a slope, so the safety program refuses the slope; it has no rule that says a vehicle is under-braked for the body it is on, and vehicles for Mars need a service brake sized for Mars gravity.
P2-E47-LIMITATION-SENTENCE: The Mars part runs the same base, roads, routes and demand with Mars gravity, a Mars Earth link and the lunar vehicles, and its encounters repeat the lunar ones on the flat (Section 6.1); a Mars site with its own terrain, roads and vehicles was planned and not run, because the terrain reader is written for the lunar polar tiles; the share of each sol with Earth in view, the conjunction date and the dust storms are assumed, and the simulated year holds a conjunction, which comes once in about 26 months, a conservative choice; and at 2,000 encounters per type the Mars bounds are five times the Moon's for the same type, 2.7 × 10<sup>−3</sup> for the unweighted types with the Bonferroni correction and up to 6.0 × 10<sup>−3</sup> for the weighted types (Table 7).
P2-H9-ABSTRACT-CLAUSE: With Earth assumed visible half of each Mars sol, referral cost one-sixth as much.
P2-CONCLUSION-MARS-CLAUSE: On Mars the rules behaved as on the Moon and referral to Earth cost about one-sixth as much; at Mars gravity the lunar vehicles' brakes hold no downhill steeper than 7.7°.

Two-way radio ranging to four surveyed beacons at the base and to as many as four other vehicles in line of sight is good to 0.3 m (Measured on Earth [64, 65]) within 100 m and to 3 m beyond that (both ranges Assumed). Its count without a margin is fixed by the design and is not a measure of safety: a waiting vehicle's window is filed to start where the conflicting window ends, so the two windows of such a back-to-back pair overlap whenever the two position errors shift them in the unfavourable order, about half the time, however small the errors are. The counts show it: at four times the fleet they were 67 to 68 a month for the three layer sets with ranging, whose 95th-percentile errors run from 32 m down to 5.8 m. Dead reckoning alone held 84, because errors of 883 m also overlapped 5 % of the pairs filed apart (before a correction to the position model, an earlier version of this paper gave 68 to 72 for all four sets). At today's fleet the count was 1.43 a month with dead reckoning alone (1.87 in the earlier version) and 0.57 to 0.73 with the other layer sets; it says how many back-to-back pairs the month held. A separate analysis of the same simulated runs measured each overlap, at today's fleet and at four and eight times (it reproduces E50's counts in every cell). Windows filed back to back, with a nominal gap under a second, overlapped in true time in 47 % to 51 % of cases at four times the fleet, where a seed holds 134 such pairs, for the four layer sets, and in 38 % to 52 % at today's fleet, where there are 42 such pairs in 30 seeds, and in 41 % to 53 % at eight times; pairs filed apart overlapped in under 1 % of cases, except with dead reckoning alone and no margin, whose errors of hundreds of metres reach them too (up to 6 %). The count therefore measures how many back-to-back pairs the month held. With dead reckoning alone at today's fleet an overlap lasted a median of 548 s and at most 2,015 s (before a correction to the position model, an earlier version of this paper gave 334 s and 1,169 s, on more overlaps). How long an overlap lasts does follow navigation: at four times the fleet the median was 483 s with dead reckoning alone, 16 s with ranging, 7.6 s with terrain fixes and 3.8 s with the navigation service of 2030. No overlap, with or without a margin, at any of the three fleet sizes, brought the two vehicles within the 5 m static margin or within R1's required gap. When the second vehicle truly entered, the first was about 440 m ahead of it (medians of 422 m to 443 m), a distance set by the length of the segments and not by navigation, and 99 % or more of the overlaps were pairs travelling in the same direction on branched segments at today's fleet and at four times, 94 % or more at eight times. An overlap is an event in the reservation accounts and not a close approach. The margin separates the filed windows, so the back-to-back overlaps go and the count falls; it does not change the gap at entry (443 m with the layered margin at four times the fleet), and the few overlaps that remain last about as long as those of the fix layer without a margin (median 4.4 s). P2-E51-MODEL-SENTENCE: Each vehicle's clock error against the base's time server is followed from its last two-way time transfer, which leaves a residual of 100 ns (Assumed) and corrects the offset but not the frequency. Two oscillator classes are compared: a temperature-compensated crystal whose frequency error is drawn uniformly from 0 to 8 × 10<sup>−7</sup>, the range the crystal of the LuGRE receiver moved through on the lunar surface (Measured [69]), and a chip-scale atomic clock at 3 × 10<sup>−10</sup> with ageing of 9 × 10<sup>−10</sup> a month (Spec [70]; the part is not space-rated). A transfer succeeds only while the vehicle has a radio path to the base mast, directly or through other vehicles. Each reservation carries a guard g at both ends, 0.1 s by default (Assumed), and a conflict caused by clocks alone is a pair of conflicting reservations whose clock errors close their stamped gap by more than 2g (Proposition 6). Ranging between vehicles is two-way, so the clock offset cancels and only the difference of the two clock rates over the 1 ms reply delay remains [71].
P2-E51-DESIGN-SENTENCE: The perfect-position runs of E50 at today's fleet, 30 seeds, with every logged reservation stamped by its holder's clock after the run, so the logistics results do not change. Oscillator class by resync interval (10 s, 1 min, 10 min, 1 h, 6 h, 1 day and never) by guard (0.01, 0.1, 1 s and none); the baseline is perfect clocks. Three variants were added after the first results and are not pre-registered: frequency steering under a daily thermal cycle, a fleet in which half the vehicles count Earth seconds [79], and the guard sweep itself.
P2-E51-RESULTS-PARAGRAPH: Table 11 gives the rows on the lunar time scale. Over 30 seeds, 303 conflicting pairs of reservations lay within an hour of each other and were checked, and 6.8 % of resync attempts found no radio path. With the 0.1 s guard the crystal caused no conflict at any resync interval from 10 s to 6 h, in any seed; it caused 1 with a daily resync and 15 with no resync. These zeros are observations and lie outside Proposition 6, whose premise is that every clock is within the guard: no crystal cell meets it. At the 6 h resync, clocks on vehicles out of radio reach were up to 0.84 s off, more than eight times the guard, and the worst of the 303 pairs closed 0.123 s of the 0.2 s that the two guards put between the windows, 62 %. No event in 303 pairs leaves a 95 % upper bound of 1.0 % per pair. With no guard, conflicts appeared at every interval and in both classes: 1 to 26 for the crystal and 22 to 25 for the atomic clock, whose largest error in any cell was 3.6 ms. That column counts signs and not sizes: with no guard the stamped gap between a waiting vehicle's window and the one before it is zero, so a pair counts as soon as its two clocks differ in the unfavourable direction by any amount, and it is a property of the count, not a result. In the guard sweep a guard of 1 s left no conflict even for a crystal that was never resynced in the month (largest error 2.14 s), 0.1 s needed a resync within 6 h and 0.01 s needed a resync within 1 h. Used for one-way ranging against the base clock, the crystal added 975 km of range error (95th percentile) at a 10 s resync and 1,787 km at 1 h; the atomic clock added 1.61 km and 3.23 km, and 42.4 km at 1 day. Two-way ranging between vehicles was off by 0.084 m with crystals and 0.11 mm with atomic clocks at the 95th percentile, with no shared clock.
P2-E51-H11-SENTENCE: H11 asks for a resync interval at which the cheaper oscillator causes no reservation conflict while its clock error still adds more than the ranging radio's own noise (0.3 m) to one-way ranging [59]: the registered rule is met at every interval from 10 s to 6 h. We report it as an observation and not as a test passed. Its second condition could not have failed: one nanosecond of clock error is 0.3 m of one-way range, so any crystal exceeds the radio's noise, and the protocol ranges two-way. Its first condition is the zero count above, which lies outside the guarantee.

P2-E54-MODEL-SENTENCE: Drop and retry sends a message end to end, tries again every 180 s and gives up after 5 tries or at the message's lifetime (Assumed). Store and forward passes custody hop by hop: the holder sends again after 10 s while the link lasts and keeps the message while there is no path. A reservation grant lives 60 s and a job award for its lease of 1 h (Assumed [80]); because the retry interval is longer than a grant's lifetime, drop and retry sends each grant once. In the replay a vehicle that has heard nothing for 600 s retraces its path at half speed to the last point where it had a link. The replay was run with the rule as first written, in which the base released a silent holder's reservation at its timeout; what it counts, the reservations whose holder was unheard 60 s after the window ended, are under the rule as stated above the segments marked unconfirmed.
P2-E54-DESIGN-SENTENCE: A replay of the month's messages over its contact plan, on the 30 seeds of E50's perfect-position runs at today's fleet: the vehicles and the base mast linked by line of sight on the terrain within radio range, step by step along the recorded trajectories, with a 14-day Earth blackout imposed. Three ways of carrying messages (drop and retry; store and forward with custody; the same with the lost-link rule) at a loss per hop of 0.10, 0.25 and 0.40. The logistics model is not run again, so a returning vehicle's detour does not change later dispatch (Section 7).
P2-E54-RESULTS-PARAGRAPH: Over the 30 seeds the month held 6,028 reservation grants and 6,028 job awards. At a loss of 0.25 per hop, drop and retry lost 1,543 grants, 26 %; with custody 2 were lost, 0.03 %. A lost grant is a vehicle stopped before a one-lane entry, because an unconfirmed reservation is never assumed. At losses of 0.10 and 0.40 drop and retry lost 9 % and 40 %. These shares are the per-hop loss itself and are a calculation on two assumed inputs, not a measurement: the retry interval (180 s) is longer than a grant's lifetime (60 s), so each grant was sent once, with a mean delay of 0.01 s. Three tries inside the lifetime would by the same arithmetic lose 0.25<sup>3</sup>, 1.6 %; that baseline was not run, so the replay does not show that custody is needed, only that a grant sent once is lost as often as a hop fails. Lost jobs, awards that expired before they arrived, were 0.33 a seed [0.17, 0.53] with drop and retry and none with custody and the lost-link rule, a paired difference of −0.33 [−0.53, −0.17]. H14 [59] has two clauses. The first, fewer lost jobs by an interval that excludes zero, is supported. The second, no reservation left stuck past its timeout, is not testable as written and is withdrawn as a result [59]: the zero followed from the rule's definition, and the rule as first written released a silent vehicle's reservation, which is unsafe when the vehicle is silent because it has failed inside the segment. Under the rule as it now stands (Section 3.11) the reservation is not released and the segment is marked unconfirmed. What the replay gives is how many those are: 2,566 of the 2,628 reservations of the month had a holder with no radio path to the base 60 s after the window ended, 7,349 h of unconfirmed segment in all, although in the replay every one of those vehicles had left its segment on schedule. An unconfirmed segment is the usual case, then, and the delay that entering it at caution speed costs has not been priced. Nor has the rest of the ladder. Along the month's contact plan vehicles had a radio path to the base mast in 56.6 % of their driving time; the replay holds 87 lost-link returns a seed against 199 jobs, and credits 365 h a seed as spent waiting, linked, at the return point; but it applies the return to the contact plan only, and the recorded job still completes. No logistics run of this paper contains the ladder (Section 7). The base's knowledge of a vehicle was 10 s old on average with the rule (worst vehicle 40 s) and 88 min without it (worst 31 h), in a replay in which a returning vehicle is given a direct link. With the rule the age is about the 10 s at which a vehicle reports its state, which is as young as it can be. Before corrections to the replay after a code review, an earlier version of this paper gave 45 s (worst vehicle 149 s), most of it a floor of half a replay step, and 82 returns and 336 h a seed.
P2-E56-DATA-SENTENCE: A's own position estimate in this experiment is simpler than the filter of Section 3.9: its error grows by 2 % of the distance driven and collapses to 1.7 m at a terrain fix, taken at every stop and about every 100 m of driving, with no filter and no terrain; the range is good to 0.3 m within 100 m (the short-range class) and to 3 m beyond (the long-range class). Five fault types are put into B's reports (sizes Assumed): a jump of 5 to 50 m, a slow drift of 0.01 to 0.5 m/s, a frozen report, a frame error of 300 to 1,000 m and report noise inflated 3 to 10 times. Fault-free data keep the honest disturbances: stops and starts, navigation error that grows and then collapses at a fix, dropouts beyond radio range, the change of ranging class at 100 m and bursts of blocked-path bias. True motion comes from 17 simulated months of the logistics model, one per seed, rebuilt at 1 Hz. The data are split by month and by vehicle pair, so that no month and no pair is in two of the training, validation and test sets; every vehicle is in all three, because a pair is assigned by the difference of its two vehicle numbers: months 1 to 6 with 28 ordered pairs for training (3,600 fault streams), months 7 to 9 with 16 pairs for validation (1,020 fault streams and 600 fault-free hours) and months 10 to 13 with 12 pairs for the test (2,000 fault streams, 400 per type, and 575 fault-free hours). An out-of-distribution set, months 14 to 17 on the test pairs, has ranging noise multiplied by 2 and dead reckoning drifting 5 % while A's filter still assumes the nominal values, with jumps of 2 to 5 m and drifts of 0.005 to 0.01 m/s, below the training range. It is one shift, chosen by us, and not a sample of the ways a sensor model can be wrong.
P2-E56-MODEL-SENTENCE: The classical test is the squared range innovation divided by its predicted variance, compared with a chi-square threshold (Proposition 5), per step and as a mean over 5 s. The other baselines are a two-sided CUSUM on the innovation and a logistic regression on 28 hand-made statistics of the last 16 and 128 s. The learned detector is a causal convolutional network: six dilated one-dimensional convolutions of 24 channels over the last 127 s of ten inputs that A can know, 9,529 parameters in all, 38 kB as 32-bit floats. It is small for three reasons. It has to run beside the safety program on a flight computer: one window takes 1.27 ms on one thread of a desktop processor, and a radiation-tolerant processor is slower by a factor we did not measure. A network of this size can be shipped as a table of weights and replayed exactly. And the search rule, fixed before the first training run, kept the smallest configuration within 0.005 of the best validation recall: the wider network tried, 16,545 parameters, gained 0.0049.
P2-E56-DESIGN-SENTENCE: Five detectors on the same streams: the per-step and windowed chi-square tests, the CUSUM, the logistic regression and the network (five training seeds). A pair-day is one ordered pair of vehicles, observer and reporter, followed for one day. For each detector the threshold is the lowest that keeps false alarms at or below one per pair-day on the validation fault-free data, a false alarm being a 60 s bin of fault-free stream with at least one alarm; a second threshold is set for one per pair-hour. Nothing is set on the test data, which were scored once. A fault is found if an alarm falls inside it, and its delay is the first alarm minus the onset.
P2-E56-RESULTS-PARAGRAPH: Table 12 gives recall and the median detection delay per fault type on the test set, 400 faults per type, at the thresholds set on validation data for one false alarm per pair-day. The realised rates on the test set were 0.53 per pair-day for the network [0.29, 0.82], 0.68 [0.18, 1.32] for the per-step chi-square, 1.26 [0.89, 1.69] for the regression, 1.35 [0.02, 4.11] for the windowed chi-square and 2.03 [1.42, 2.77] for the CUSUM. The intervals are from 1,000 resamples; an earlier version of this paper gave them on the first 200 (the network's was [0.29, 0.82]). They are wide because the rates rest on few alarms: the fault-free test data are 575 one-hour blocks drawn from four strata and weighted back to 24 pair-days, and one alarm-minute in the heaviest stratum (70 % of natural time, 152 blocks) is 0.11 per pair-day. The recalls below are therefore at one nominal rate and not at exactly equal realised rates. Over all faults the network found 90 %, the regression 86 %, the CUSUM 77 % and the two chi-square tests 71 % and 70 %. Every detector found frame errors (99.5 % or more). The network found 100.0 % of the noise-inflation faults against the per-step chi-square's 35.5 %, and 92.0 % of jumps against 69.8 %. Slow drifts were the hard type: the best recall was 63 % (the windowed chi-square test), so every detector missed at least 37 % of them. The network did not beat the logistic regression everywhere. On jumps it found 92.0 % against 95.5 % (difference −0.035 [−0.054, −0.019]). On slow drifts its median delay was 85 s against the regression's 81 s and the CUSUM's 78 s, differences whose intervals include zero. At the looser rate of one false alarm per pair-hour the regression found 95 % of all faults and 78 % of drifts, the network 94 % and 73 %.
P2-E56-H15-PARAGRAPH: H15 is four tests at one false alarm per pair-day [59]. (a) On slow drifts the network's median detection delay is shorter than the per-step chi-square test's: held. The delays were 85 s and 109 s, a difference of −24.1 s [−35.1, −14.9], at the lower realised false-alarm rate (0.53 against 0.68 per pair-day); recall was 61.8 % against 57.5 %. Each median is over the faults that detector found; on the faults both found the paired difference was −23.2 s [−26.8, −19.9]. (b) On jumps the two are within one second: failed, in both directions. The network was 1.2 s later (90 % interval [1.0, 1.6], which reaches past the 1 s margin), and it found more jumps, 92 % against 70 % (+0.22 [0.18, 0.26]). The registered expectation, no better on jumps, was wrong. (c) Against the CUSUM, with no predicted direction: on slow drifts the delay differed by 6.4 s [−3.1, 15.9], no difference, and recall by +0.053 [0.026, 0.080]; on jumps recall differed by +0.15. The CUSUM's realised false-alarm rate was 2.0 per pair-day. (d) Out of distribution the network's recall may fall below the CUSUM's: by the numbers it did, and the comparison means little. At the deployed thresholds the network found 22.6 % of the small jumps and 11.3 % of the slow drifts, the CUSUM 66.5 % and 66.5 %. These recalls are not at one false-alarm rate, because no detector kept its rate: the network gave 13.8 false alarms per pair-day, 26 times its test rate, the regression 18.3, and the three innovation tests 199 to 863; the per-step chi-square test's rate rose 700 times. A false alarm is a minute with an alarm, so the CUSUM's 1,016 per pair-day in the long-range class is 71 % of all fault-free minutes, and a detector that alarms that often meets most faults by coincidence: there it “found” 98 % of the small jumps with a median delay of 18 s, against 0 s on the test set. In the short-range class, where it gave 28 false alarms per pair-day, it found 20 % of the small jumps and 13 % of the drifts; the network found 21 % and 5 % at 3.3 (Table 12, by ranging class). The detections of the innovation tests out of distribution cannot be told from their false alarms. The events show the same. A fault counts as found if an alarm is on during it, whether or not the alarm was already on, and out of distribution an alarm had been raised in the 60 s before the fault began in 50.7 % of the CUSUM's events, 28.5 % of the per-step chi-square test's and 4.0 % of the network's. On the events with no alarm in that minute, recall over all fault types was 69.3 % for the CUSUM, 73.2 % for the per-step chi-square test and 65.1 % for the network, against the 84.2 %, 79.2 % and 66.0 % over all events that Table 12 and an earlier version of this paper give. With thresholds reset on half of the out-of-distribution fault-free data (realised rates 0.7 to 1.9 per pair-day on the other half), no detector found these two fault types (1 % to 3 %), so nothing separates the detectors there. The network kept the frozen, frame and noise faults (96 %, 100 %, 100 % at the deployed thresholds).
P2-E55-DESIGN-SENTENCE: The protocol's rule exactly as written [80]: the per-step chi-square test at the theoretical threshold γ = 10.83 (α = 10<sup>−3</sup>, Proposition 5), a report declared suspect when three of the last five tests are flagged, and nothing tuned on any data; scored on the validation, test and out-of-distribution streams of E56 with E56's event scoring, beside the single test at the same threshold. Because no parameter of the rule is chosen on data, scoring it on the test set chooses nothing there, and the set stays scored once for every tuned detector. For agreement, the trimmed-mean rule of Proposition 7 runs on the radio mesh of the terrain: 5, 8, 12, 20 and 40 rovers, at positions drawn from the fleet's trajectories or spread evenly over the route samples; honest values with a spread of 1 m; 0 to 2 faulty rovers that send values 50 m off in opposite directions (Assumed); the rule's parameter F set to 1 and to the number of faulty rovers; 60 steps and 50 runs a cell.
P2-E55-RULE-PARAGRAPH: E55 scored the protocol's rule as written on the same streams. On the test set it gave 0.10 false alarms per pair-day and found 67.7 % of all faults (73.5 % of jumps, 61.8 % of slow drifts and 8.5 % of noise inflation), against 71.3 % for the per-step test calibrated on validation data and 90.3 % for the network (Table 12). The single test at the same threshold, without the persistence rule, gave 53 false alarms per pair-day. A false alarm of 10<sup>−3</sup> per test, at one test a second, is up to 84 minutes with an alarm in a day for independent Gaussian innovations, so the persistence clause is what brings the theoretical threshold under one false alarm per pair-day on these data. The single test alarmed in fewer minutes than that, here and at the next threshold (4.8 against 8.6 at γ = 15.14), and the rule's own rate is far above the 0.0009 a day that independent tests would give: the innovations are neither independent nor Gaussian with the claimed variance, and flags arrive in runs. The rule's rate is a handful of alarm-minutes in 575 fault-free hours; the results file keeps neither their count nor an interval. No alarm-minute fell in the heaviest stratum, where a single one would be 0.11 per pair-day, and no alarm in that stratum's 152 hours still allows up to 0.33 per pair-day from it at 95 %. Out of distribution the rule gave 69 false alarms per pair-day and found 26 % of the small jumps and 25 % of the slow drifts; the single test gave 1,128. A Monte Carlo check of Proposition 5 in the same code flagged an error of 4.57 σ<sub>v</sub> with probability 0.900 at a false alarm of 0.98 × 10<sup>−3</sup>.
P2-E55-H16-PARAGRAPH: For agreement, in all 30 cells in which F was at least the number of faulty rovers, every honest value stayed inside the initial honest range at every step of every run, on meshes that met the robustness condition and on meshes that did not (20 cells without it, none with a run that left the range). With more faulty rovers than F (two against F = 1) the range held in 48 % to 66 % of runs at fleet positions and in 70 % to 92 % of spread runs. Agreement, the honest range shrinking below 1 % of its first width in 60 steps, was reached in 0 % to 10 % of runs where F covered the faulty rovers, and in no more than 10 % with no faulty rover at all; the largest share in any cell, 18 %, is with two faulty rovers and F = 1, where the rule is not safe. The mesh is sparse: every honest rover heard the 2F + 1 others the rule needs in 0 % to 30 % of fleet runs and in none of the spread runs. H16 as registered has two halves [59]: on a (2f+1)-robust mesh every run stays inside the honest range, and on a mesh that is not, at least one run leaves it. The first half held and the second did not, so H16 is not supported as written. The second half mis-stated the theory, which a dated change of [59] records: the rule's safety needs no more than F faulty neighbours of each honest rover, on any graph, and robustness decides whether the honest rovers converge (Proposition 7). That restatement was written after the result and is exploratory.
P2-E55-MAST-SENTENCE: A variant run after these results adds the base mast to the mesh as one more honest node, linked to every rover it can see. At fleet positions the graph was then connected in 58 % to 96 % of runs, against 0 % to 10 % without it, and agreement was reached in 0 % to 16 % of runs against 0 % to 10 % (cells with F at least the number of faulty rovers); every run stayed inside the honest range. With the rovers spread over the routes nothing changed: the graph was connected in at most 8 % of runs and no run agreed. The mast makes the graph a star, and a rover that hears the mast and one or two others can have every value it hears trimmed away. More links help only while F covers the faulty rovers. With two faulty rovers and F = 1 at fleet positions the range held in 2 % to 24 % of runs with the mast, against 48 % to 66 % without it (6 % against 50 % with 12 rovers): the mast connects the faulty rovers to more honest ones.
P2-B97-PARAGRAPH: One check uses real data. The same detector family, with none of its thresholds and without the network, was run on the labelled SMAP and MSL telemetry of the telemanom data release [82], taken from a public mirror whose label file is byte-identical to the original: 82 channels and 105 labelled anomalies in all, of which the first 14 channels of each spacecraft, with 38 labelled events, were used. This is housekeeping telemetry of a satellite and a Mars rover. It is not lunar rover position data, and it tests one thing only: whether a detector that accumulates evidence finds more than a per-step test on real signals. The channels are the first 14 of each spacecraft in the order of the file listing, a subset set by download size and not by any property of the channels. The detectors are of E56's family and not at E56's settings: the window is 16 steps against 5, and the CUSUM has a reference of 0.5 without centring against 3 with centring. Each channel is standardised on its own training data, and each detector's threshold is its largest score on that training data, so nothing is set on the labelled events. On the level of the signal the windowed chi-square and the CUSUM found 13 and 13 of the 18 MSL events against the per-step test's 10, and 12 and 16 of the 20 SMAP events against 2 (Table 13). Their precision was 0.38 to 0.46, with thresholds that were not tuned per channel. The comparison is not at one false-alarm rate: on SMAP the two accumulating detectors raised 18 and 26 runs of alarms that touch no labelled event, against the per-step test's 2. The z-score and per-step columns of Table 13 are one detector on a single channel and print the same numbers. On the first difference of the signal the accumulating detectors found no more than the per-step test (10 and 10 against 10 on MSL; 7 and 5 against 7 on SMAP). The first difference is the residual closest to an innovation, so on the signal that most resembles the one the traffic rules test, accumulation gained nothing. The check supports no choice of detector, and we draw none from it. The logistic regression and the network take the ten features of a vehicle pair and do not apply to a single telemetry channel. The published results of the study that released the data are not quoted: we did not open that paper, and these numbers do not reproduce it.
P2-FAMILY-STATS-SENTENCE: [59] names a family of confirmatory hypotheses, H9′, H10′, H13, H14 and H15 (a), for a Holm correction at α = 0.05. H9′ and H13 are comparisons with a threshold and have no sampling test; they are reported by the share of seeds or draws on the predicted side, and H13 belongs to the companion papers. The correction is applied over the three that have a test: H10′ by paired two one-sided tests at today's fleet, joined with its other two clauses by intersection and union, so that its p value is the largest of the three; H14 by an exact sign test on the lost jobs per seed; and H15 (a) by the bootstrap over events, whose p value is the count of resamples at or above zero plus one, over the number of resamples plus one. These p values are not registered: [59] gives its decision rules by interval, and the three tests were constructed after the results so that the correction could be applied. The sign test is one-sided (two-sided p = 0.0039), and the registered rule for H14, a paired interval that excludes zero, gives the same verdict. Over the registered family of five, counting the two hypotheses that have no test, the adjusted values would be at most 0.005 for H15 (a) and 0.008 for H14, and no verdict changes.

Its first clause holds (p below 0.001), but the one-sided p value is 0.87 for a larger gap at four times the fleet, 0.66 at eight times, and 0.17 for a costlier dead-reckoning margin at today's fleet, and the three clauses joined have a Holm-adjusted p of 0.87. P2-PROP1-NUMBERS: With m = d<sub>0</sub> = 5 m and the drift of Section 3.9, σ<sub>ε</sub> = 2 % gives d* ≤ 250 m and 10 % gives 50 m; the two-sided 95 % level, 1.96 σ, is reached after at most 128 m and 26 m. P2-PROP2-NUMBERS: The premise is about speed as well as position. A vehicle is at each end of the segment within β/v of the time it believes only if it covers the stretch of length β there at the speed v. A vehicle that starts from rest at a bay, as every waiting vehicle does, needs √(2β/a) to cover β at its acceleration a: 6.5 s for β = 4.3 m and a = 0.2 m/s<sup>2</sup>, against a margin β/v of 1.0 s at 15 km/h. And a waiting vehicle whose position is wrong by β may stand up to β inside the mouth of the segment for as long as it waits, which no margin in time covers; a stop line set back from the entry by β does. Neither is in the rule as it was run: the logistics model takes v as the mean speed of the whole leg and has no stop line. Errors of opposite sign on the two vehicles are covered by the proof.
P2-PROP3-NUMBERS: On the Moon g = 1.62 m/s<sup>2</sup>, so friction allows a = μg = 0.73 m/s<sup>2</sup> on the flat at μ = 0.45; R2 uses the smaller of that and the 0.5 m/s<sup>2</sup> service brake, and d<sub>0</sub> = 0 inside the sight distance. With 0.5 m/s<sup>2</sup> and 20 m of clear sight, a vehicle that reacts on board after 1 s may drive at 14.4 km/h; one whose driver is on Earth and reacts after 6 s, the middle of the 4 to 8 s delays NASA tested [78], at 8.6 km/h. With 10 m of sight the two caps are 9.7 km/h and 4.9 km/h, and with the friction limit alone (a = 0.73 m/s<sup>2</sup>) at 20 m they are 17.0 km/h and 9.3 km/h. NASA's simulator study measured a mean of 2.03 km/h at a 6 s delay [78], below these caps, which is consistent with them and validates nothing. At long delays the term a t<sub>r</sub> dominates and friction hardly matters; at short delays it does. R2 computes the distance as the proposition does, at constant speed through the reaction time; R1's gap lets the follower accelerate at a<sub>acc</sub> through it, which is the more cautious. The same formula gives the caution speed of the lost-link rule (Section 3.11). A vehicle that enters a segment marked unconfirmed may find a stopped vehicle in it, so it drives no faster than v<sub>max</sub> for its own perception range d<sub>p</sub>, with the static margin d<sub>0</sub> = 5 m kept: 6.4 km/h for d<sub>p</sub> = 10 m, 12.3 km/h for 20 m, and the 15 km/h class limit from 27 m on, with the on-board reaction time and the service brake on the flat. No model in this paper has run that speed.
P2-PROP4-NUMBERS:
With bmax = 0.8 m/s2 and d0 = 5 m the final gap is negative for a leader faster than 2.83 m/s (10.2 km/h); at 15 km/h the shortfall is 5.9 m. A follower that keeps its own full stopping distance, 23.3 m + d0 at 15 km/h in place of 12.5 m + d0, needs no assumption about the leader; we did not run that rule. E44 found the case: in 58 of 10,000 encounters with a nonconforming vehicle the follower came inside the 5 m static margin, and in 7 it touched, all with a leader stopped dead by a fault (Section 5.6).

Assumption (vii) also fails for a vehicle that breaks no rule. Guaranteed braking is b = min(bservice, μg cos θ) − g sin θ with θ positive downhill, so a leader that brakes fully on an uphill grade decelerates at bservice + g sin|θ|, which exceeds bmax = 0.8 m/s2 on grades steeper than 10.7° on the Moon and 4.6° on Mars (where the service brake binds; at μ = 0.3 on the Moon friction binds and the grade is 11.5°). The steepest slope on the base's routes is 17.2°. By the formulas above, at 15 km/h a follower at exactly dmin behind a leader that brakes fully on that grade ends 3.0 m from it on the Moon: inside the 5 m static margin, which is a hard violation by this paper's own definition, with no fault and no rule broken. At Mars gravity on the same grade the final gap is 0.2 m. That is the worst case of the formulas, a follower that accelerates through its whole response time.

Uphill encounters were then simulated: following on a two-lane road and a convoy inside one one-lane segment, at lunar and Mars gravity, on grades of 5°, 10°, 15° and 17.2°, 2,000 encounters a cell, with every follower held at the rule's limit, once with commands that act at once, as in the main run, and once with an actuation lag of 1 s, R1's response time. Under R1 as it was, no vehicle touched another in any cell, but followers came inside the 5 m static margin, which is a hard violation. On the Moon this happened only when following with the lag, from 14° (14 of 2,000 encounters at 15°, 335 at 17.2°, smallest gap 4.15 m), and never in the one-lane convoy. At Mars gravity with the lag it happened from 6.5° when following and 8.5° in the convoy, down to a gap of 0.72 m, and at 15° and above even without the lag. With a slope term in R1, the leader's braking taken as the larger of bmax and its guaranteed braking on the grade, no follower came inside the margin when following, on either body, at any grade, with or without the lag. In the Mars convoy with the lag 71 of 2,000 encounters at 15.0° and 62 of 2,000 encounters at 17.2° still ended inside it, by at most 0.14 m (smallest gap 4.86 m). A trace puts that remainder on the lag model, in which a vehicle that commands braking still applies one 0.1 s step more of its earlier commands than R1's response time allows; it was not patched. An R1 breach, which is not a hard violation, is counted in the cells with the lag only when the gap has been below R1's required distance for longer than the response time of 1 s while the braking the vehicle applies is still short of full, which is what R1 asks; by that count none of the 32 cells with the lag had a breach. Counted on the command at once, as the results first were, five of them had breaches in 0.05 % to 15 % of encounters, all of them followers that braked within the response time. Cells without the lag keep the count on the command. Part (b) as stated, with a fixed bmax, is therefore established for the flat and for downhill grades only, which is where the twelve encounter types were driven. With the slope term, (vii) reads “no harder than the larger of bmax and its guaranteed braking on the grade”, the proof goes through unchanged, and the simulation agrees with it when following. R1 with the slope term is the rule we propose (Table 2); in the code it is an option, and the twelve types were run without it, on the flat and downhill, where it changes nothing. Two more things are assumed without being listed. Part (b) takes the follower to know the true gap and the leader's speed; under position error the widened gap d0 + k bAB of Section 3.9 is meant to cover that, and the encounters did not exercise it. And part (a) is close to the definition of the rule: (iii) assumes that a vehicle has left by the end of its window, which a vehicle disabled inside the segment has not. That case is outside (a) as well as (b). What covers it is the lost-link rule of Section 3.11: the segment stays reserved, is marked unconfirmed, and is entered only at the caution speed of Proposition 3.
P2-PROP5-NUMBERS: For one range and α = 10<sup>−3</sup>, γ = 10.83 (z = 3.29); for a range and a bearing, γ = −2 ln α = 13.82. A report wrong by b along the line of sight is flagged with probability 0.9 once b reaches 4.57 σ<sub>v</sub> and with 0.99 at 5.62 σ<sub>v</sub>. With navigation errors of 2 m on both vehicles and a ranging error of 0.3 m, σ<sub>v</sub> = 2.84 m: the threshold is 9.4 m and the error found nine times in ten is 13.0 m; R9's fixed tolerance of 11 m lies between them. If three of the last five tests must be flagged, and the tests are independent, a false alarm has probability 1.0 × 10<sup>−8</sup> per window and an error flagged with 0.9 per test is declared with 0.991. E56 bears on the assumption twice. At one report a second, one false alarm a day is α = 1/86,400 and γ = 19.2; the threshold found on validation data, with none of the Gaussian argument, was 19.1. That is one point at which the two tails cross and not a test of the law: at the lower thresholds the same test alarmed less often than Gaussian innovations would (Section 5.11). And when the true errors were larger than the variance the filter claimed, the same threshold gave 479 false alarms per pair-day (Section 5.11): the false-alarm rate is only as good as S. The independence in the three-of-five clause does not hold on those streams either: E55 measured 0.10 false alarms per pair-day for the rule, against 0.0009 for independent tests.
P2-PROP7-NUMBERS: E55 tested part (a). In all 1,500 runs with F at least the number of faulty rovers, every honest value stayed inside the first honest range at every step, whether or not the mesh was robust; with two faulty rovers and F = 1, where the premise can fail, the range held in only 48 % to 92 % of runs, by cell. Part (b) is stated from [72] and E55 does not test its sufficiency: only 12 of the 800 meshes small enough for an exact check were (2F+1)-robust, and agreement was reached in at most 10 % of runs in any cell in which F covered the faulty rovers (Section 5.11).
P2-PROP6-NUMBERS: A clock with frequency error y, resynced every τ to a residual r, has |x| ≤ |r| + |y|τ, so it stays within g while τ ≤ (g − |r|)/|y|: for g = 0.1 s and the crystal's 95th-percentile frequency error that is 36.5 h, and the drawn clocks of E51 held it for 36.7 h. In all 51 cells of E51 in which the largest clock error was within the guard, on the two time scales, no conflict occurred, as the proposition requires: 42 atomic-clock cells and 9 crystal cells with the 1 s guard. No crystal cell with the 0.1 s guard is among them, because vehicles out of radio reach miss their resyncs, so the zero conflicts that Section 5.10 reports for that guard lie outside this proposition: at the 6 h resync the largest error was 0.84 s and the worst pair closed 0.123 s of the 0.2 s between its windows. The premise is sufficient, not necessary: at a 10 s resync the crystal's largest error was 0.33 s, on vehicles out of radio reach, yet the clocks closed no gap between two conflicting reservations by more than 18 µs, because those vehicles held no reservation next to an opposing one at the time. That zero is an observation on 30 seeds; the guarantee is the proposition's.
P2-H7-ABSTRACT-SHORT: The safety program allowed no violation in ten of twelve encounter types, all flat or downhill: a vehicle that stops dead in a one-lane segment defeats the gap rule, and one landing closure in 10,000 left a vehicle inside the zone. Uphill, a braking leader took followers inside the 5 m margin, without contact; a slope term removed this when following, leaving up to 0.14 m in a Mars convoy with a 1 s lag.
P2-P6-ABSTRACT-CLAUSE: Without satellites, ranging held position error inside the 5 m margin where two beacons were in sight (23 % of driving) but not over the registered radio range (49 m); terrain fixes left 15 m elsewhere, and their stops, not reservation margins, set the cost: 0.65 h per delivery (a lower bound). With a 0.1 s guard, clocks up to 0.84 s off caused no conflict in 303 reservation pairs, outside the guarantee. A network found slow drifts 24 s sooner than a chi-square test, but every detector missed at least 37 % and none kept its false-alarm rate with noisier sensors, so none qualifies for the safety path.
P2-P6-INTRO-PARAGRAPH:
The second set of experiments removes four assumptions of the first: that every vehicle knows where it is, that all clocks agree, that every message arrives and that every reported position is true. They are replays of one recorded month; the encounters and the exhaustive check were not run again. Without a navigation satellite service, ranging to four beacons kept the 95th percentile of position error at 4.3 m, inside the 5 m the rules set aside, where two or more beacons were in line of sight. That is 23 % of the driving, and a reading of the registered “within radio range of the base beacons” that we chose after the results; within radio range as registered, which is all of the driving, the error was 49.1 m and the clause failed in every seed. Terrain fixes left 15 m away from the base, so one clause of the positioning hypothesis failed and the verdict on another depends on the reading (Section 5.9). A reservation widened by the vehicle's own 95 % bound, 38 s at each end with the layered estimate, changed delay per delivery by +0.007 h. The stops for terrain fixes that the estimate needs, 37 h a month or 23 % of the fleet's driving time, raised it by 0.65 h (3.7 %) when a follow-up run put them into the logistics model, and that figure is a lower bound. The count of reservation overlaps, which we first read as a safety result, is fixed by the design and is reported only as a count. With a guard of 0.1 s on each reservation a crystal clock resynced within six hours caused no conflict in 303 conflicting pairs; this is an observation outside the guarantee we prove, since clocks out of radio reach were up to 0.84 s off (Section 5.10).

Message custody kept reservation grants from being lost, against a baseline that by its assumed timing sent each grant once. A silent vehicle's segment is not released: it is marked unconfirmed and may be entered only at caution speed, a rule adopted after an internal review and not yet run, and 2,566 of the month's 2,628 reservations ended with their holder unheard (Section 5.12). A network of 9,529 parameters found wrong position reports sooner and more often than the chi-square test on held-out data at the same nominal false-alarm rate; every detector missed at least 37 % of slow drifts; and when the sensors were noisier than in training no detector kept its false-alarm rate, so none is qualified for the safety path on this evidence (Section 5.11). The protocol's own rule, the same test at its theoretical threshold with three of the last five tests flagged, gave 0.10 false alarms per pair-day on the test set without tuning and 69 with the noisier sensors; and trimmed averaging among rovers never left the range of the honest values while its parameter covered the faulty rovers, but converged in at most 10 % of runs on our sparse mesh, so one registered hypothesis about it failed as written. Seven propositions in Appendix A state what follows from the rules by argument alone, each with its assumption, and Section 8 lists every claim as proved, tested, calculated from assumed inputs, assumed or not yet tested.
P2-P6-DISCUSSION-POSITION: The later experiments asked what the rules need from navigation, from clocks and from the honesty of reports. On position the answer divides at the edge of the beacons' coverage. Where two or more beacons are in line of sight, 23 % of the driving, two-way ranging keeps a vehicle within the 5 m that R1 already sets aside. That is a reading we chose after the results. Under the registered wording, within radio range of the base beacons, the error is 49.1 m and the second clause of H9′ fails in every seed; with one or more beacons in sight it is 12.5 m and within 1 km of the mast 25.1 m. Ranging to four beacons at the base, then, holds the margin only where two of them are seen at once. Elsewhere terrain fixes leave a 95th-percentile error three times the margin (Table 9); the weak places are the dark legs, where fix opportunities are 500 m apart and 30 % of fixes fail, and the loose slopes, where dead reckoning drifts 10 %. What a margin sized by each vehicle's own bound buys in safety we cannot yet say. Proposition 2 guarantees disjoint windows while each error stays inside its bound and the vehicle passes the ends of the segment at speed, and E50 counted how often the filed bound was exceeded (Table 10). The count of overlaps without a margin is fixed by the way back-to-back windows are filed and measures no hazard: no overlap, with or without the margin, brought two vehicles within the static margin, and the first vehicle was about 440 m ahead when the second entered. The margin removes overlapping windows from the reservation accounts; it does not move vehicles further apart. What the margin costs is clearer. With the layered estimate it is 38 s at each end and the widened windows cost 0.007 h per delivery at today's fleet; with dead reckoning alone it is 25 min at today's fleet, where its cost of 0.10 h was not resolved, and 27 min at four times the fleet, where it cost 1.9 h per delivery. The layered estimate, though, depends on stops for terrain fixes, 37 h a month, and with those in the logistics model the delay per delivery rose by 0.65 h, 3.7 %, a lower bound because the model inserted only part of the stop time (Section 5.9). The cost of positioning without satellites is the stops, not the margins. Two of the three clauses of H10′ were not supported, and the experiment resolved neither: at four times the fleet ten seeds do not settle the layered margin's difference, and at today's fleet the dead-reckoning margin cost more in 23 of 30 seeds while its mean could not be told from zero. The pre-registration said that a failure of H10′ would mean that position error sets traffic capacity [59]; these runs neither show that nor exclude it.
P2-P6-DISCUSSION-TIME:
On time, clock quality matters for one-way ranging long before it matters on the roads, and the protocol ranges two-way. The guard of 0.1 s is less than a hundredth of the position margin. With it a crystal resynced within six hours caused no conflict in 303 pairs, but that is an observation and not the guarantee: Proposition 6 needs every clock within the guard, clocks out of radio reach were up to 0.84 s off, and the worst pair used 62 % of the two guards between its windows. A design that wants the guarantee must size the guard to the largest clock error it tolerates; in this sweep a guard of 1 s covered the crystal's largest error up to a six-hour resync. The lost-link experiment shows two things and prices neither in delay. A lost grant is a stopped vehicle, because R3 never assumes an unconfirmed reservation. The 26 % of grants that drop and retry lost at a loss of 0.25 per hop is that loss itself: its retry interval is longer than a grant's lifetime, both assumed, so each grant was sent once, and three tries inside the lifetime would by arithmetic lose 1.6 %. Custody removes the loss; the replay does not show that it is needed. And a silent vehicle is the usual case: along the month's contact plan vehicles had a radio path to the base in 57 % of their driving time, and 2,566 of 2,628 reservations ended with their holder unheard. Under the rule as first written the base released those segments, which is unsafe when the holder is silent because it has failed inside one; under the rule as it now stands they are marked unconfirmed and entered only at caution speed. No logistics run contains the lost-link ladder. The fleets of E43 and E50 never turn back, the replay holds 87 returns a month against 199 jobs, and the nearest thing that was priced, the strict reading of R7, cost 49.1 h per delivery. The delay cost of the ladder and of caution-speed entry is therefore unknown and probably large.

On integrity, the network did what H15 (a) asked and more on jumps and noise, at the same nominal false-alarm rate on held-out data. Out of distribution, when the true sensor errors were larger than the filter claimed, no detector kept its false-alarm rate, so their recalls there cannot be compared and no choice of detector follows from them. The three innovation tests gave 199 to 863 false alarms per pair-day and the network 14. A detector that alarms in most minutes meets most faults by coincidence: in the long-range class, where the CUSUM alarmed in 71 % of fault-free minutes, it found 98 % of the small jumps; in the short-range class, where it gave 28 false alarms per pair-day, it found 20 %, against the network's 21 % at 3.3. The classical tests lost more of their calibration than the network (the per-step test's rate rose 700 times, the network's 26), and with thresholds reset to the nominal rate every detector found 1 % to 3 % of the small jumps and slow drifts. R9 turns each false alarm into an inflated volume and a delay, and no run prices false alarms at these rates, so failing towards alarms is not shown to be the safe direction. On this evidence none of the detectors is qualified for the safety path. What the chi-square test has is a threshold that follows from a stated assumption (Proposition 5); what the experiment shows is that the assumption, the claimed variance, is the thing to monitor. No detector helps with slow drifts, of which every one missed 37 % or more: a single range sees only the error along the line of sight, and a second witness at another bearing is needed. No experiment here has two witnesses cross-check one report. E55 adds two observations. The protocol's rule as written gave 0.10 false alarms per pair-day on the test set without tuning, because of its persistence clause: the same threshold alone alarmed in 53 minutes of a day. That rate rests on a handful of alarm-minutes and has no interval, and with the noisier sensors it was 69. And agreement among rovers by trimmed averaging does not work on this terrain: the rule cannot be pushed outside the honest range while F covers the faulty rovers, and more links do not make up for an F that is too small (Section 5.11), but the honest rovers converged in at most 10 % of runs, 16 % with the base mast as a node, because few of them hear three others. On this mesh a shared estimate, such as the position of a beacon or a hazard, cannot be left to averaging among rovers. Computing it at the base, with the trimmed mean kept as a fallback that cannot be pushed outside the honest range, is the design these results point to; it was not run.
P2-P6-CONCLUSION-CLAUSE: Without satellites, ranging held position error inside the 5 m margin only where two beacons were in sight; the stops for terrain fixes set the cost, 0.65 h per delivery as a lower bound; and no detector of wrong reports kept its false-alarm rate with noisier sensors.
P2-CONCLUSION-SAFETY-SHORT: One safety program enforcing ten rules, tested in simulation, allowed no violation in ten of twelve encounter types, all flat or downhill; a vehicle that stops dead in a one-lane segment defeats the gap rule, and one landing closure in 10,000 left a vehicle inside the zone. A ring of one-lane segments deadlocked in 13 of 1,892 encounters (0.7 %) under the rule as written and in 373 of 1,963 (19.0 %) with a variant. Uphill, a braking leader took followers inside the static margin, without contact; a slope term in the gap rule removed this when following, and a Mars convoy with a 1 s lag kept shortfalls of at most 0.14 m.
